turns.prompt_text: is it possible to write a comment within a terminal command on Mac?
turns.response_html:
Yes, it is absolutely possible to include comments within a terminal command on macOS (which uses the Zsh shell by default).

Depending on whether you are writing a single-line command or a complex multi-line script, there are two primary ways to do this:

1. The Standard Hash Method (#)

In Zsh and Bash, the # character signals the start of a comment. Everything following it on that line is ignored by the shell.

  • At the end of a command: mkdir Project_Alpha # Creating the main directory for the launch
  • On a new line: 
    # Update the system packages before starting
brew update

[!IMPORTANT]
If you are typing a single-line command, you cannot put a comment in the middle of the command (e.g., cp #source file1 #destination file2) because the shell will stop reading the command as soon as it hits the first #.

2. Multi-line Commands with Comments

If you are writing a longer command using the backslash (\) to break lines, you can tuck comments in between the lines. This is common in DevOps and software engineering to explain complex flags.

docker run -d \
  --name web-server \
  -p 8080:80 \
  # This maps the internal port 80 to 8080 on your Mac
  nginx:latest

3. The "Hidden" Comment Trick (Inline)

If you absolutely must put a comment inside a one-line command without breaking it, you can use a no-op (no operation) command or a variable trick, though this is less "natural" than the #:

  • Using a : (The No-Op): The colon : is a built-in command that does nothing. You can use it to "store" a comment if you use backticks or command substitution. echo "Hello World" $(: This is an inline comment)

Summary Table

MethodSyntaxBest Use Case
Hash# commentEnd of lines or dedicated comment lines.
Backslash\ # commentMulti-line commands (Docker, complex installs).
No-Op$(: comment)When you need a comment strictly inline (rare).

The fish shell (Friendly Interactive Shell) handles comments very similarly to Zsh or Bash, but there is one major technical difference you should know regarding where you can place them.

1. The Standard Hash (#)

Just like other shells, the # character is the primary way to comment in fish. Anything after it on the same line is ignored.

  • Example: mkdir New_Project # Creates the directory for the 2026 launch

2. The "No Inline" Rule

In fish, the # must be at the beginning of a line or preceded by a space. You cannot put it immediately after a command without a space, or it might be interpreted as part of a filename or string.

  • Correct: ls -a # Show hidden files
  • Incorrect: ls -a#Show hidden files (Fish may try to look for a file named -a#Show)

3. Multi-line Comments (The Key Difference)

One of the "friendlier" things about fish is how it handles multi-line commands. Unlike Zsh, where you often need a backslash (\) to continue a command onto the next line, fish often detects when a command is unfinished (like after a pipe |).

However, you cannot put a comment on the same line as a backslash continuation in fish.

  • ❌ This will fail in fish: 
    echo "Hello" \ # This comment breaks the command
"World"
  • ✅ This works in fish: 
    # First we echo the greeting
echo "Hello" \
"World"

Comparison Table

FeatureZsh/Bash (Mac Default)Fish Shell
Basic Comment# Comment# Comment
Inline (End of Line)SupportedSupported (requires space before #)
After Backslash \SupportedNot Supported (breaks the escape)
Piped Comments`ls# comment` (Valid)

[!TIP] Since fish is designed to be "helpful," it will actually dim the color of your comments automatically as you type them, making it visually obvious that the shell is ignoring that text.

turns.prompt_text: I'm using ocrmypdf, my PDF has pages that are out of order. It's a PDF of JPEG images, but each page is out of order.
turns.response_html:
Since you are already using ocrmypdf, you likely have a workflow that involves the command line. Correcting the page order of a PDF made of JPEGs is a common headache, especially if the file names or scan order didn't line up.

Depending on how many pages you have and how they are "out of order," here are the three most efficient ways to fix this on your Mac.

1. The "Quick Fix" (Preview.app)

If the PDF only has a few pages (10–20), using macOS’s built-in Preview is the fastest way without running more code.

  1. Open your PDF in Preview.
  2. Go to View > Thumbnails.
  3. Drag and drop the page thumbnails in the sidebar into the correct order.
  4. Press Cmd + S to save.
  5. Now run ocrmypdf on this newly ordered file.

2. The "Power User" Way (qpdf or pdftk)

Since you are comfortable with the terminal, you can use qpdf (which ocrmypdf actually uses under the hood). This is best if you know the specific sequence (e.g., "I need page 3 to be page 1").

Install qpdf

brew install qpdf

Reorder Pages

If you want to reorder a 4-page PDF to be 4, 1, 2, 3:

qpdf --empty --pages input.pdf 4,1-3 -- output_ordered.pdf

3. The "Scripter" Way (If JPEGs are separate)

If you still have the original JPEG files and they are named in a way that is logically sortable (like scan_1.jpg, scan_10.jpg, scan_2.jpg), the computer might be sorting them "alphabetically" rather than "numerically."

You can use the img2pdf engine to bind them in the exact order you want before running OCR:

# Install img2pdf
brew install img2pdf

# Use a wild card to grab them in order
img2pdf *.jpg -o combined.pdf

# Then run your OCR
ocrmypdf combined.pdf final_searchable.pdf

Which "Out of Order" are we talking about?

ScenarioRecommended Tool
Randomly jumbledPreview (Manual Drag & Drop)
Specific pattern (e.g., even pages then odd)qpdf or pdftk
Original JPEGs existimg2pdf with a sorted list

[!TIP] If your pages are upside down or sideways, ocrmypdf has a specific flag for that: ocrmypdf --rotate-pages input.pdf output.pdf

Is there a specific pattern to how they are out of order (like every other page), or is it completely random?

turns.prompt_text: So they are randomly ordered, jumbled; however, they do have the page numbers on them.
turns.response_html:
If the pages are already in a single PDF but the numbers printed on the actual pages don't match the current digital order, you have two main routes: the Manual Visual route or the Automated OCR route.

Since you are already using ocrmypdf, you have a powerful engine at your disposal to potentially automate this.

Option 1: The "Visual Sort" (Recommended for < 30 pages)

Since they are "randomly" jumbled, the fastest way to get them right without writing a complex script is to use the Contact Sheet view in macOS Preview.

  1. Open the PDF in Preview.
  2. Press Cmd + Opt + 6 (or go to View > Contact Sheet).
  3. This gives you a grid of all pages. Because the page numbers are printed on them, you can quickly spot "Page 1," "Page 2," etc.
  4. Drag and drop the thumbnails into the correct order.
  5. Save (Cmd + S) and then run ocrmypdf.

Option 2: The "OCR-First" Automation (Advanced)

If you have hundreds of pages, sorting by hand is a nightmare. You can actually use ocrmypdf to "read" the pages first, then use a script to rename/resort them based on the text it found.

The Strategy:

  1. Run OCR on the jumbled mess: ocrmypdf jumbled.pdf ocr_temp.pdf
  2. Extract text per page: Use a tool like pdftotext (part of the poppler brew package) to create individual text files for every page.
  3. Search for "Page X": Write a small script (I can help with this) that looks for the string "Page" followed by a number in those text files.
  4. Rebuild: Use qpdf to stitch them back together in the discovered order.

Option 3: If you still have the JPEGs

If the JPEGs are separate files, the "random" order usually happens because of how the scanner named them (e.g., img_1.jpg, img_10.jpg, img_2.jpg).

You can use a Renamer tool or a simple zsh loop to rename them. On a Mac, you can:

  1. Select all JPEGs in Finder.
  2. Right-click > Rename...
  3. Use "Format" to give them a consistent naming scheme like page_001.jpg, page_002.jpg. This often forces them into the correct sequence if they were originally scanned in order but named poorly.

Which way sounds better for your specific file?

  • Manual: I'll just drag them around in Preview.
  • Automated: There are too many pages; help me write a script to find the "Page X" text.

How many pages are in this PDF?

turns.prompt_text: So actually, when I scanned them, I scanned them. All of the front side, so all odd numbers, and then I scanned all of the back side, so all even numbers. So the first half of the pages will all be odd, and the second half of the pages will all be even, or the opposite of that.
turns.response_html:
This is actually a classic "duplex scanning" problem! You don’t need to sort these manually or write a complex OCR script. Since the pages follow a strict mathematical pattern, you can use a tool called pdftk (the PDF Toolkit) to "interleave" them.

If you have 10 pages total, your PDF currently looks like: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 (or the reverse).

Step 1: Install the tools

The easiest way to do this on a Mac via the terminal is using pdftk-java.

brew install pdftk-java

Step 2: The "Shuffle" Command

If the first half of your PDF is the "Fronts" and the second half is the "Backs," you can split the file and then shuffle them together.

Assume your file is jumbled.pdf and has 20 pages total (10 fronts, 10 backs):

# 1. Extract the front pages (1-10) into one temp file
pdftk jumbled.pdf cat 1-10 output fronts.pdf

# 2. Extract the back pages (11-20) into another temp file
pdftk jumbled.pdf cat 11-20 output backs.pdf

# 3. Shuffle them together (1 from fronts, then 1 from backs, etc.)
pdftk A=fronts.pdf B=backs.pdf shuffle A B output ordered.pdf

Wait—Are the back pages in reverse order?

Often, when you flip a stack of paper over to scan the backs, the scanner reads them from the last page to the first (e.g., 10, 8, 6, 4, 2).

If your "even" pages are in reverse order, use the output modifier to flip them back before shuffling:

# Extract the backs in reverse order (10 down to 1)
pdftk jumbled.pdf cat 20-11 output backs_reversed.pdf

# Now shuffle
pdftk A=fronts.pdf B=backs_reversed.pdf shuffle A B output ordered.pdf

Why do this before ocrmypdf?

You should definitely run this shuffle before running ocrmypdf.

  1. Logical Flow: OCR engines work better when they can process text in the intended reading order (especially for multi-page tables).
  2. File Size: It's more efficient to OCR the final, corrected document once than to try and rearrange OCR'd metadata later.

Do you know if your "even" pages were scanned in the correct order (2, 4, 6...) or if they came out reversed (10, 8, 6...)?

turns.prompt_text: Correct, the back ones are in reverse order. the first ones, even ones are in forward order
turns.response_html:
Since your back pages are in reverse order, we have a perfect mathematical fix. We will split the PDF into two halves, flip the second half, and then "zip" them together like a deck of cards.

Since you're on a Mac and already comfortable with the command line (given you're using ocrmypdf and fish), here is the exact workflow using pdftk-java.

1. Install PDFTK

If you haven't yet, grab the toolkit:

brew install pdftk-java

2. The Solution Script

Let's assume your PDF has 50 pages total (meaning 25 front-side pages and 25 back-side pages). You can run these commands directly in your terminal:

# 1. Grab the first 25 pages (Odds: 1, 3, 5...)
pdftk input.pdf cat 1-25 output fronts.pdf

# 2. Grab the last 25 pages and REVERSE them (Evens: 50, 48... becomes 2, 4, 6...)
pdftk input.pdf cat 50-26 output backs_corrected.pdf

# 3. Interleave (Shuffle) them together
pdftk A=fronts.pdf B=backs_corrected.pdf shuffle A B output final_ordered.pdf

How to calculate the numbers for your file

To make sure you use the right page ranges, use this simple logic:

  • Total Pages: $N$
  • Split Point: $H = N / 2$
  • Fronts: 1 to $H$
  • Backs (Reversed): $N$ down to $H + 1$

Example: If you have 32 pages:

  • Fronts: 1-16
  • Backs: 32-17

Pro-Tip: The "Fish" way

Since you are using the fish shell, you can actually set variables to make this reusable if you have to do this often:

set total 50 # Change this to your total page count
set half (math $total / 2)
set half_plus_one (math $half + 1)

pdftk input.pdf cat 1-$half output fronts.pdf
pdftk input.pdf cat $total-$half_plus_one output backs.pdf
pdftk A=fronts.pdf B=backs.pdf shuffle A B output fixed.pdf

Next Step

Once you have fixed.pdf, you can run your ocrmypdf command on it. The text will now be in the correct logical order for searching and copy-pasting.
